So before you open the first session, sit with me a while, because this study will only go as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the answers. It is settling your own heart, and being honest with yourself about your own questions. The aim of this series is narrow and it is hard. It is to take the hardest questions faith faces, the suffering, the silence, the reliability of the book, the failures of the church, the doctrine of hell, the apparent quarrel with science, and to take them seriously enough that an honest person can sit in the room and not have to lie. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to win every argument. It is not to send everyone home with their doubts cured and a bow on top. It is not to protect God, who does not need you to protect him, and who took the worst question a human being ever asked into his own mouth on the cross. If anyone leaves this study feeling that their real questions were dodged or shamed, the study failed, however orthodox the answers sounded. Keep that in front of you, because the single greatest danger you face as a leader of a study on doubt is the urge to rescue, to fix, to swoop in with the answer the moment someone says the frightening thing. Resist it. A question rushed to an answer is a question that has been told it was not welcome. Here is the most important thing you will hold all the way through, and the man who wrote this study built the whole thing on it. He came to faith from atheism. He remembers the inside of unbelief, not as a cartoon but as a real and reasonable place he actually lived, and he was raised without a father, which means he knows from the inside what it is to wonder whether anyone is up there at all. Write doubt from the inside, the way he does. Never strawman unbelief. When you state a hard question, state it at its strongest, the way the smartest skeptic you know would state it, before you go anywhere near an answer. If you have to weaken the objection to answer it, you have taught the room that the faith cannot survive the real one, which is the opposite of what you came to do. The study is built to model this, every objection is steel-manned before it is engaged, and you must protect that even-handedness with your life, because the skeptic in the room can smell a rigged fight from across the table, and the moment he smells one, he is gone, and he was right to go. Now the careful line that runs through every session, and you must hold it without turning it into a weapon. There is a difference between honest doubt that seeks God and deconstruction that is really an exit. But that line is not a sorting hat, and it is not yours to apply to other people. It is a mirror, first for you, then offered gently to each person for their own use. Honest doubt stays in the room with God, arguing, accusing, refusing to leave, the doubt of the father who cried help my unbelief. The harder forms of deconstruction have already decided and are narrating the reasons. The test is direction, not intensity, not volume, not how angry the question is. But you do not get to announce that someone has crossed the line. The instant you use the distinction to dismiss a person, you have proven the leaver's worst suspicion, that the church only calls it honest doubt when it ends back in the pew. Use the line on yourself out loud, and let the room watch you do it, and let everyone else apply it to their own heart in the quiet. Now keep the room safe, because depth requires safety and doubt is one of the least safe things a person can confess in a church. People have hidden these questions for years, sometimes decades, terrified that saying them out loud would be the thing that finally broke their faith or got them quietly written off. Safety here does not mean comfort. It means a person can say the true thing, the really frightening thing, without being fixed, shamed, argued at, or prayed over as if they were a problem to be solved. Make four things explicit in the first session and guard them every session after. First, there are no questions that are off limits here, none, including the one you are most afraid of. Second, doubting is not sinning, and nobody is in danger of hell for the questions they bring to this table, Jude says have mercy on those who doubt and we are going to obey that verse. Third, we are not here to fix anyone, so if you came to be fixed you can relax, and if you came to fix someone else you can stop. Fourth, what is said here stays here. Set those four and the room will slowly exhale, and the real conversation, the one people have been carrying alone, can finally begin. Here is the part that matters most for the kind of room you may be walking into, and it is the reason this study exists. You may have a real skeptic in the room, someone who is not a believer and is not pretending to be, who came because a friend asked or because they are genuinely searching or because they want to be honest in a place that usually punishes honesty. And you may have someone who is actively de-converting, losing their faith in real time, sitting in your group with the floor moving under them. These are not problems to be managed. These are the people the study was written for, and how you treat them will teach the whole room more than anything you say. Do not perform delight that they came and then spend the hour trying to win them. Do not let the group gang up on them, even gently, even with love, because six believers and one doubter is not a conversation, it is an ambush. Make it genuinely safe for them to say the hard thing, by saying a hard thing yourself first, by naming your own real doubt out loud, by granting the full force of their objection before anyone offers a response, and by being completely willing to say I don't know when you don't know. The fastest way to lose a skeptic is to pretend you have an answer you do not have. The fastest way to keep one is to be more honest than they expected a Christian to be. If the de-converting person decides, in your room, that they can be in the middle of losing their faith and still be loved and still be welcome at the table, you have done something most churches never manage, whatever they decide about God in the end. Watch the clock and the temperature together. Silence after a hard question about doubt is almost always a person deciding whether it is safe to say what they actually think. Count to ten, count to twenty, before you rescue it. Let the silence do its work. And when an answer is genuinely hard, when someone asks the suffering question with a fresh grave behind it, slow down, stop teaching, and be a human being in the room before you are a leader of it. Some of these sessions will not resolve, and they are not supposed to, because Bell does not resolve them and neither does Scripture, which gives us Job with no explanation and Habakkuk with the fig tree bare. Trust the closing prayer to carry what the discussion could not. End every session there, even when nothing felt finished, because a room sent out carrying its questions toward God will come back changed in a way a room sent out with tidy answers never will. Now the part it would be easiest to skip, your own heart. You cannot lead people into honest doubt if you are pretending you have none. If you walk in as the one who has it all figured out, the strong believer helping the weak doubters, you have already failed, because you will lead from above the room instead of inside it, and the doubters will feel the distance and close back up. So before session one, go looking in yourself. Name the question you have never said out loud. Find the place where your own faith is held together with tape. Locate the doubt you have been protecting God from because you were secretly afraid he could not survive it. If you cannot find any real question in yourself, you are either not being honest or you have not loved God long enough to have suffered with him yet, and either way you are not ready to lead this until you have gone looking. The leader who has doubted can welcome the doubter without fear or contempt. The leader who has only ever performed certainty will turn the study into a defense of his own fragile position, and the room will know. Here is your charge. You are not the answer-man and you are not the gatekeeper of anyone's faith. You are a fellow doubter who happens to be holding the questions, walking people toward a God who went into the fire ahead of all of you and came out. Lead like that. Let the hardest questions land on you first and hardest. Refuse every chance to win cheaply, to strawman the skeptic, to fix the hurting, to use the line between doubt and deconstruction as a weapon against anyone but yourself. Make it safe to say the true thing, by saying yours first. And when you do not know, say so, because your honest I don't know will keep a skeptic in the room that your best argument would have driven out. The goal is not a room with no questions left at the end. The goal is a room full of people, you first, who have learned that they can bring their whole divided heart to a God who is not afraid of it, and who would rather have them in the room arguing than gone and certain. Go gently. Go honestly. Go first, into the fire, where he already is.

faq.q: Is this study going to try to talk me out of my doubts or fix me?
faq.a: No, and if it feels like that is happening, the leader has misread it. The study is built on the conviction that doubt brought to God is not a malfunction to be repaired but, in its honest form, one of the deepest expressions of faith. The man at the center of the first session cries I believe, help my unbelief, and Jesus helps him without first making him resolve the contradiction. Jude tells the church to have mercy on those who doubt, and this study is an attempt to obey that verse. You will not be cornered, you will not be shamed, and nobody here thinks you are in danger of hell for the questions you carry. What you will find is your hardest questions stated at full strength, taken seriously, and walked through honestly, with plenty of room left for the parts that do not resolve, because Scripture leaves them unresolved too.

faq.q: I am not a Christian. Will I be welcome, or am I just a project?
faq.a: You are welcome, and the study was written with you specifically in mind. The author came to faith from atheism, so he is not pretending to find your position foreign or stupid, he lived in it and remembers it as a real and reasonable place. The whole study is built to state the skeptic's case at its strongest before any answer is offered, which is the opposite of a setup. You are not a project to be closed and you will not be ganged up on, because six believers aiming at one skeptic is not a conversation, it is an ambush, and a good leader will not allow it. Come to be honest in a place that usually punishes honesty. You can disagree out loud, you can find the answers insufficient and say so, and you will still be at the table next week. The only thing asked of you is that you take the questions seriously, which you already do.

faq.q: What is the difference between honest doubt and deconstruction?
faq.a: The study draws the line carefully, and it refuses to make it a weapon. Honest doubt stays in the room with God. It argues, it accuses, it weeps, but it keeps bringing the questions to him rather than only about him, the way the psalmist accuses God to his face without leaving, the way Job refuses to either curse God or pretend. Deconstruction, in its harder form, has already decided to leave and is reverse-engineering the reasons for going. The test is the direction the questions point, not how intense or angry they are, because the loudest doubter may be the one holding on hardest. But the study is emphatic that this line is a mirror for your own heart, not a label to pin on other people, and it grants fully that a great deal of what people deconstruct was never the gospel to begin with, but a culture, a politics, or an abuse wearing the gospel's clothes. Leaving that is not the same as leaving Christ.

faq.q: Does the Bible actually treat doubt as acceptable, or is that just modern softness?
faq.a: It is in the text, not imported into it. The father in Mark is helped in his unbelief. Thomas is given the wounds to touch rather than thrown out for needing evidence. The psalmist asks how long will you hide your face, will you forget me forever, and the complaint is preserved as Scripture. Habakkuk opens his book screaming at God for doing nothing. Job argues for thirty-seven chapters and is told at the end that he, the accuser, spoke rightly while his theologically tidy friends did not. John the Baptist doubts Jesus from a prison cell and Jesus answers him with evidence and a blessing, not a rebuke. And Jude tells the whole church to have mercy on those who doubt. The Bible is far less nervous about honest doubt than the modern church often is. What it warns against is not the question brought to God but the hardness that has decided to walk away from him.

faq.q: If God is good and powerful, why is there so much suffering, and does this study pretend to answer that?
faq.a: It does not pretend, and that is the point. The session on suffering refuses the cheap answers, the it-was-for-a-reason that turns a death into a lesson, the everything-happens-for-a-purpose that makes God the author of the tumor, because those answers protect the comforter and wound the sufferer, and the skeptic who rejects them is often more honest than the believer who recites them. The study states the problem of suffering at full philosophical strength and then shows what Scripture actually does with it, which is not to hand over a proof but to hand over Habakkuk, who gets a vision and a command to wait instead of an explanation, and the cross, where God himself enters the silence and cries why have you forsaken me. That does not solve the logical problem, and the study admits it. What it changes is who is in the room when you ask the question. You are no longer shouting at a God who has never felt what you feel.

faq.q: Why is God so silent? If he wanted a relationship, would he not answer?
faq.a: The study takes that argument seriously and calls it serious, not stupid, because the most economical explanation of a silence really can seem to be an absence. It grants that the silence is real, that it has driven sincere people away, and that the believer who has never felt it has probably never prayed hard enough to hit it. Then it shows what Scripture does with the same silence, which is strange for a book supposedly invented to comfort the gullible. It does not deny the silence. It canonizes the complaint about it, in the Psalms and in Habakkuk, putting the accusation against God into the mouth of the worshiper. And it locates the deepest silence in the Bible inside God himself, on the cross, where the Son cries out and the Father does not answer. The Christian claim is not that the silence is fake or that you imagined it. It is that God has been inside it, which is a different thing than absence.

faq.q: Can I trust the Bible when there are contradictions, variants, and hard texts?
faq.a: The study takes the reliability question as real and not a test of loyalty, and it refuses the apologetics that overpromise, because the everything-harmonizes-perfectly approach is exactly what shatters when a young person finally reads honestly. It grants the genuine difficulties, the textual variants, the tensions between accounts, the texts used to do real harm. Then it asks what the skeptical case cannot account for, the embarrassing details no inventor includes, the women as first witnesses in a world that did not admit a woman's testimony, the disciples written as cowards and fools, the cry of dereliction left in. It notes that the manuscript tradition behind the New Testament is earlier and better attested than any other ancient text by an enormous margin, and that the tensions between accounts behave like independent testimony rather than a smoothed-out fabrication. You do not get a guarantee every detail harmonizes. You get a book that survives being read with your eyes open.

faq.q: How does the study deal with the violent and morally troubling parts of the Bible?
faq.a: It does not flinch and it does not contort, because both are what make those texts lethal. It grants that the hard texts are hard, that the conquest reads like genocide and some passages regulate rather than abolish slavery, and that the history of using these texts to justify atrocity is real and damnable and demands a repentance the church has mostly refused. Then it does the work the objection usually skips, reading the texts in their genre and ancient context rather than as a modern field manual, noticing how the law restrains and humanizes practices the surrounding cultures took for granted, and following the arc the canon bends across itself, from regulation toward release, from the household codes toward there is neither slave nor free, the arc the abolitionists read correctly and the slaveholders had to ignore. The Bible does not float above its bloody world untouched. It moves against the grain of it, and it indicts the men who weaponized it more sharply than its critics do.

faq.q: I left the church because of how its people treated me. Does this study just defend the institution?
faq.a: No. The session on the church grants the wound at full weight and refuses to defend the indefensible, because defending it is the very hypocrisy under indictment. The abuse is real, the cover-ups are real, the harm runs down through generations, and the study says plainly that the people who left over it were often more offended by what offends God than the people who stayed and made excuses. Then it makes one distinction, that the betrayal of Christ by his church is not an argument against Christ, it is the argument Christ made first and hardest, calling the religious leaders whitewashed tombs and a brood of vipers in words sharper than any modern critic has used. The hypocrisy lands on the hypocrite. It does not touch the one he betrayed. The study invites you to separate, in your own mind, the Jesus who wept over the city from the people who wounded you in his name, and to bring him the injury rather than only the verdict.

faq.q: How can a good God send people to hell? Is that not enough to reject the whole thing?
faq.a: The study takes the moral revulsion seriously and refuses to make it easy, because a God who tortured people forever for finite sins, or for being born in the wrong place, would be a monster, and the gleeful way hell has been preached as a whip for the frightened deserves the contempt it gets. It grants all of that. Then it looks at what the doctrine, taken with care, actually involves, that the warnings come overwhelmingly from Jesus himself and almost always aimed at the religious insider rather than the outsider, and that the most serious thinkers have understood hell less as a torture chamber God operates and more as the terrible honoring of a freedom, a door locked from the inside. And the center is the cross, where the God who warns of judgment took the judgment into himself rather than handing it down from a safe height. He is not dispensing a fate he refused to face. He faced it first. The study admits you may still find the doctrine hard, and says that is all right.

faq.q: Are faith and science really at war, and do I have to choose?
faq.a: The study calls the war story a bad one, mostly built on a category confusion that serves neither honest science nor honest faith. It grants that specific churches have fought specific findings badly and embarrassed themselves. But science asks how the mechanism works and faith asks what it means and whether there is anyone behind it, and these are two different questions, not rival answers to one. The men who founded modern science, Kepler, Newton, Faraday, Maxwell, were largely believers who felt no contradiction, because they did not confuse the how with the why. Honest science does not require atheism, and honest faith does not require you to be ignorant. The conflict is real only at the edges, where one side reaches over to answer the other's question and calls the trespass a victory. You do not have to choose between using your mind and keeping your faith, and anyone who told you that you did was selling something.

faq.q: What if I go through this whole study and still have doubts at the end?
faq.a: Then you will be in good company, because that is exactly where the study ends, and on purpose. The last session does not pretend the questions were all solved, because a faith that needed everything solved was never going to survive the first real winter. It points instead to Job, who argued with God for thirty-seven chapters, never got his explanation, and was restored anyway with the words now my eye sees you, the encounter standing in for the answer he demanded. And to Thomas, who doubted hardest and worshiped deepest, out of the very wound he insisted on touching. The faith the study commends is not the one that never asked. It is the one that went through the fire and came out holding God rather than holding answers. So if you finish with questions still in your hands, the study would call that a success, provided the questions are still being carried toward God and not used as the reason to walk away from him.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have doubts of my own and no theological training?
faq.a: Your doubts are not a disqualification, they are your way in, and the study was built to be led by an ordinary person rather than an expert. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, every objection is already stated at its strongest and answered, and the leader primer walks you through the hard moments, including how to lead a room with a real skeptic or a de-converting person in it. The one thing the study asks of you is not training and not having your own faith perfectly resolved. It is willingness to go first, to name your own real question out loud, to make the room safe by being more honest than people expected a Christian to be, and to say I don't know when you do not know, because that honesty will keep a skeptic in the room that your best argument would have driven out. Read the primer, settle your own heart, and trust the material to carry the rest.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you in particular if you came carrying something heavy. Before we start, four things. First, there are no off-limits questions at this table, none, including the one you are most afraid to say. Second, doubting is not sinning. Nobody here is in trouble with God for the questions they brought, and the Bible literally tells the church to have mercy on those who doubt, so that is what we are going to do. Third, we are not here to fix anyone. If you came to be fixed, you can relax. If you came to fix someone else, you can stop. Fourth, what is said here stays here. The man who wrote this study came to faith from atheism, so he is not going to pretend your hardest questions are stupid, and neither am I. We are going to state the hard things at full strength before we say anything back to them, because a faith that has to cheat to win was never worth keeping. Tonight we are sitting with this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at the question itself, and we have not pretended it away. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the actual week we are walking into, because none of this matters if it stays an argument about other people's faith.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because Scripture does not resolve it either. It gives us Job with no explanation and Habakkuk with the fields bare, and a God who went into the fire himself. So take the weight of this out with you rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. Bring your questions to God this week instead of only carrying them alone. Let me pray for us before we go, and I will see you next time. Thank you for the courage it took to be honest in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the four ground rules of safety, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, The Difference Between Doubt and Deconstruction, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, When God Hides, part one, the problem of suffering and the refusal of the cheap answers.
Week 4: Session 2 continued, the hiddenness of God, Habakkuk, and the cross as God entering the silence, plus practice.
Week 5: Session 3, Can You Trust the Book, Scripture under question.
Week 6: Session 4, When the Church Wounds, hypocrisy.
Week 7: Session 4 continued, the doctrine of hell, with extended time on the cross and the judge judged in our place.
Week 8: Session 5, Faith on the Other Side of the Fire, integration, the science question, and what each person carries out.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the difference between doubt and deconstruction and the question of suffering and silence.
Week 2: Session 3, Can You Trust the Book, with extended time on the hard texts and the embarrassing details.
Week 3: Session 4, When the Church Wounds, hypocrisy and hell held together.
Week 4: Session 5, Faith on the Other Side of the Fire, plus a short integration close.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, The Difference Between Doubt and Deconstruction.
Week 2: Session 2, When God Hides, Suffering and the Silence.
Week 3: Session 3, Can You Trust the Book, Scripture Under Question.
Week 4: Session 4, When the Church Wounds, Hypocrisy and Hell.
Week 5: Session 5, Faith on the Other Side of the Fire.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's raw journal of doubt and rage after his wife's death, a believer accusing God to his face and refusing to leave. Anchors the lament of session 2. The honesty is the point, not the resolution.

bibliography.title: The Problem of Pain
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's more measured treatment of suffering and of hell as a door locked from the inside, the self-exclusion God grievously honors. Used in sessions 2 and 4. Read alongside A Grief Observed for the head and the heart of the same man.

bibliography.title: Can We Trust the Gospels?
bibliography.author: Peter J. Williams
bibliography.note: A careful case for the reliability of the Gospel accounts, the undesigned coincidences and the marks of eyewitness testimony. Central to session 3. Leader to confirm specific claims before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: The Crucified God
bibliography.author: Jürgen Moltmann
bibliography.note: The argument that God himself enters the godforsakenness of the cross, so the cry of dereliction happens inside the Trinity. Grounds the reversal in session 2. A demanding book, offered as the theological depth behind the claim that God entered the silence.

bibliography.title: The Great Divorce
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's parable of hell as self-chosen, the refusal of heaven by souls who will not surrender their grievance. Supports the account of hell in session 4 as freedom grievously honored rather than torture dispensed.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The ancient record of a restless, questioning mind moving toward God through doubt rather than around it, our hearts are restless until they rest in you. Background for the whole study's vision of faith that has asked.

bibliography.title: Night
bibliography.author: Elie Wiesel
bibliography.note: Wiesel's account of faith shattered in the camps, the silence of God at its most unbearable. Offered so the study never treats the problem of suffering as a thought experiment. Leader to handle with care and never to answer glibly.

bibliography.title: The Brothers Karamazov
bibliography.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
bibliography.note: Ivan's argument from the suffering of children is the strongest statement of the problem of evil in literature, and Dostoevsky, a believer, refuses to weaken it. A model for steel-manning the objection. Supports session 2.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The accessible case for the reasonableness of the faith, useful for the seeker working through whether belief can be held with intellectual honesty. A balancing constructive voice across the study.

bibliography.title: Faith After Doubt
bibliography.author: Brian D. McLaren
bibliography.note: A sympathetic account of deconstruction from inside the experience, valuable for understanding why people leave and what they are reaching for. Offered as a voice the study engages rather than endorses. Leader to confirm before attributing any claim to Bell's own position.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: On the disposition of Christ toward the weak, the wavering, and the doubting, the heart that does not break the bruised reed. A pastoral counterweight to any harshness, useful in sessions 1 and 4. Leader to confirm specific claims before citing.

furtherReading: The Reason for God, Timothy Keller, for the reader who wants the fuller even-handed case behind every session, each hard objection granted before it is answered.
A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for anyone in fresh grief who needs to know a believer was allowed to rage at God and stay, read alongside session 2.
Can We Trust the Gospels, Peter Williams, for those who want to think harder about the historical reliability of the accounts behind session 3, leader to confirm specific claims.
The Great Divorce, C. S. Lewis, for readers wrestling with hell who want the picture of judgment as freedom grievously honored rather than torture dispensed, read with session 4.
The Brothers Karamazov, Fyodor Dostoevsky, for those willing to hear the problem of suffering stated by a believer at its most unanswerable, the way honest faith must be willing to hear it.

glossary.definition: The honest questioning of faith that brings its hard questions to God rather than only about him, and refuses to leave the room. Not the same as unbelief. Scripture treats it as something to be handled with mercy, not suspicion.

The taking-apart of an inherited faith. In its honest form it discards what was never the gospel and keeps Christ. In its harder form it has already decided to leave and is reverse-engineering the reasons. The test the study uses is direction, not intensity.

The settled refusal of God, the heart that has decided no, distinct from doubt, which still reaches toward him. The father in Mark confesses both faith and unbelief in one breath and is helped, which shows even unbelief can be brought to Jesus.

Any attempt to justify the goodness and power of God in the face of suffering. The study refuses the cheap versions that explain away a person's pain, and notes that Scripture offers not a theodicy but a God who enters the suffering himself.

The philosophical problem that a God who desires to be known stays silent and unseen, which some take as evidence of his absence. The study grants the argument is serious and answers it with the lament psalms and the silence God himself enters on the cross.

The biblical prayer that accuses God of silence or absence and refuses to leave the room, as in Psalm 13 and Habakkuk. Scripture canonizes the complaint against God, putting the accusation into the mouth of the worshiper and calling it prayer.

The historical principle that details which embarrass the writer, the women as first witnesses, the disciples written as fools, the cry of dereliction, are unlikely to be invented and so point toward genuine testimony rather than propaganda.

Jesus' cry from the cross, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, itself a quotation of Psalm 22. The deepest experience of God's silence and abandonment is taken into God himself, so the question now lives inside the Trinity.

The understanding of hell less as a torture chamber God operates and more as the terrible honoring of a freedom, a door locked from the inside, the self-chosen refusal of the only source of life. Held alongside the cross, where God bore the judgment himself.

The popular story that faith and science are inherently at war. The study calls it a category confusion, since science asks how the mechanism works and faith asks what it means, and notes that many founders of modern science were believers.

To state an opposing argument in its strongest possible form before answering it. The study steelmans every hard objection on purpose, because a faith that can only beat a weakened version of the question has not actually survived the real one.

Bell's name for the doubt that seeks God, the father's I believe help my unbelief, the doubt that stays in the argument like Job until it sees God. One of the deepest forms of faith, not its failure or its enemy.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Most churches handle doubt by not handling it, and the questions go underground and the people go with them. This five-session study does the opposite. It takes the hardest questions faith faces, suffering, the silence of God, the reliability of Scripture, the failures of the church, the doctrine of hell, the quarrel with science, and states each one at full strength before saying a word back. It is written from the inside of unbelief by a man who came to faith from atheism, it never shames the doubter, and it makes a careful, fair distinction between honest doubt that seeks God and deconstruction that is really an exit. Built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Come with your real questions, not your performed certainty.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a five-week study on doubt, and before anyone braces, hear this. It is not a study that will shame you for having questions, and it is not a study that pretends the questions are easy. It takes the hardest objections to the faith, suffering, the silence of God, the hard parts of the Bible, the wounds the church has caused, and the doctrine of hell, and it states them honestly before it answers them. There are no off-limits questions, doubting is not sinning, and nobody will be fixed against their will. If you have been carrying a question alone because you were afraid to say it out loud, this is for you. No homework, and no prep needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: The church often acts like doubt is the opposite of faith. The Bible does not. The man who cried I believe, help my unbelief went home with a healed son. A five-session study on doubt, deconstruction, and the God who is not afraid of either, honest enough to state the hardest questions at full strength and to start with the leader's own. Come with your real questions, not your performed certainty.
quoteCards: Doubt and unbelief are not the same thing. Unbelief walks away from God. Doubt walks toward him with its hands full of questions.
The church that panics at hard questions has confused its own fragility with God's.
The cheap answers protect the person saying them, not the person bleeding.
Habakkuk does not get his question answered. He gets a God to trust inside the unanswered question.
The Bible is not a book that asks to be trusted blind. It is a book that survives being read with your eyes open.
The betrayal of Christ by his church is not an argument against Christ. It is the argument Christ made first, and made hardest.
He is not dispensing a fate he refused to face. He faced it first, and he faced it for us.
The faith worth having is not the one that never asked. It is the one that went through the fire and came out holding God.
